title: Hypotheses, IV & DV
examples: What is the difference between a hypothesis and a theory?
Can you give an example of operationalising a concept?
How do I know if my hypothesis is directional?

explain.say: Today we are learning about forming good research hypotheses. A hypothesis is an educated guess about a relationship between things.

draw.text: Hypothesis: Educated guess about a relationship.

explain.say: First we must learn about operationalising concepts. This means defining abstract ideas using measurable terms. For example, we might measure 'anxiety' by counting heart rate.
Next we look at the independent variable or IV. This is the variable that the researcher changes or manipulates. For instance, we might change the amount of sleep given to a group.
The dependent variable or DV is what we measure to see if it changes. If we change sleep, we might measure test scores as the DV. Test scores are what depend on sleep.
A directional hypothesis predicts the specific way the variables relate. For example, more sleep will lead to higher test scores. It predicts a direction.
A non-directional hypothesis predicts there is a relationship but not the direction. It just says the variables are linked. For example, there is a link between sleep and scores.

faq.q: What is the difference between a hypothesis and a theory?
faq.a: A hypothesis is a specific, testable guess about a relationship. A theory is a much broader explanation supported by a large body of evidence.
asks: Is a hypothesis the same as a prediction?
How is a theory different from a guess?

faq.q: Do I always have to operationalise everything?
faq.a: Yes, in scientific research, you must operationalise abstract concepts. This makes sure your variables can actually be measured in the real world.
asks: What is the purpose of operationalising?
Can I skip operationalising in my study?

faq.q: When do I use a directional versus non-directional hypothesis?
faq.a: Use directional when you have strong prior research suggesting the direction. Use non-directional when you are unsure of the direction of the link.
asks: Which type of hypothesis is stronger?
Do I need to know the outcome before writing the hypothesis?

faq.q: What is the independent variable in a study on diet and mood?
faq.a: The independent variable is the thing you change, which would be the type or amount of diet given to the participants.
asks: How do I identify the IV?

faq.q: If I change the IV, does that automatically prove my hypothesis?
faq.a: No, changing the IV only allows you to test the relationship. Correlation does not prove causation in research.
asks: What is the difference between correlation and causation?

facts: A hypothesis must be testable using empirical evidence.
The independent variable is the cause or the factor being manipulated.
Operationalising turns abstract ideas into measurable variables.
A directional hypothesis predicts the specific nature of the relationship.

quiz.say: If a researcher changes the amount of study time and measures test scores, what is the independent variable?
quiz.why: The study time is the factor the researcher deliberately changes or manipulates.

wrong.0: The participants are the subjects, not the variable being changed.
wrong.2: This is the outcome being measured, making it the dependent variable.
wrong.3: The relationship is what the hypothesis predicts, not a variable itself.

quiz.say: If a researcher measures 'aggression' by counting the number of times a child hits a doll, what process are they using?
quiz.why: They are taking the abstract idea of aggression and giving it a concrete, countable measurement.

wrong.0: Controlling variables means keeping them the same, not defining them.
wrong.1: Analyzing data happens after the measurements have been taken.
wrong.3: Hypothesizing is making the guess, not defining how to measure it.
